narration.text: Ask a leading language model to add two three-hundred-digit numbers, and it's usually right.
Here, one digit is wrong, and the answer gives no warning.
Passing yesterday's tests doesn't guarantee tomorrow's answer.
What if we could check every step a small model could ever take?
This is Sketchpad: a model that reads pictures and text, with about eight hundred million learned numbers, or weights, running in your browser.
Watch it multiply, divide, factor a polynomial, and open a sheet inside a chat reply.
None of this calls a calculator or a tool. Every digit is computed by the model itself.
How does it do that?
Like school arithmetic, it works on a sheet, one column at a time.
Each step sees only three printed cells and an instruction, never the whole problem or earlier steps.
From that tiny image come a digit, a carry for the next column, and the next step.
Simple code writes those outputs and moves the window.
We trained about ten million extra weights—a small add-on called LoRA—while keeping the original model fixed.
Why show it so little?
Longer numbers need more steps, but no new kinds of window.
There are only two thousand, four hundred and forty-six possible views, counting the instructions.
We can check every one.
But does getting every window right mean getting the whole calculation right?
Yes, provided the code presents the right views: a correct step sets up the next correct step.
Lean, a computer proof checker, checks our proof for every length.
Written reasoning that rereads earlier steps keeps creating new situations; we also proved that finite testing alone cannot certify all those histories.
There's a practical catch: computers round numbers, and different chips round differently.
If the right digit wins by a hair, rounding could change the winner.
So we measure its lead over the strongest wrong answer—the margin—and check every view in the browser on a laptop's graphics processor.
The smallest lead was three point zero two.
Rounding would have to move a score by more than half of that, one point five one, to flip a digit; running views together in batches moved scores by at most one point zero nine.
That repeatable record of the checks and margins is the certificate.
And on whole problems?
On two hundred and twenty sums and products fixed in advance, Sketchpad answered all two hundred and twenty; the strongest of ten other models answered two hundred and seventeen.
Without its sheet and adapter, the same small model answered twenty-three.
Those checked procedures can also work together.
A short program factors this cubic—a polynomial whose highest power is three—with every computed number coming from the model.
The ordinary code arranging the steps and moving the view remains outside the proof.
But people ask questions, not just calculations.
So we trained a chat version to reach for its sheet by itself.
First, the original model coached it on replies it wrote itself; then we rewarded it whenever its sheet gave the right answer.
Because the skill is an add-on, a dial called the gate can switch it off: at zero, the original model returns, bit for bit.
Chat keeps that dial on, and there's a cost: on fresh grade-school word problems, it scores five point eight percentage points below the original.
We can also ask where a multiplication digit takes shape inside the model.
At different processing layers, we pushed its internal state toward another digit.
Through layer fifteen, no tested answer changed; just after layer twenty, all eighty tested multiplication answers changed.
Now give it two long numbers and watch it work.
It rechecks its weakest windows on your graphics processor; the full check is available for a new device.
The paper, code and model are open.
